live_web_research.page_text: [2609.31403] Sorry Robot, Happy Human: Vision-Language Models Read Only One of Two Legible Typographic Layers Skip to main content Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Computation and Language arXiv:2609.31403 (cs) [Submitted on 25 Sep 2026] Title: Sorry Robot, Happy Human: Vision-Language Models Read Only One of Two Legible Typographic Layers Authors: Mert İncidelen , Yamen Kashkash , Asya Berker , Murat Aydoğan View a PDF of the paper titled Sorry Robot, Happy Human: Vision-Language Models Read Only One of Two Legible Typographic Layers, by Mert \.Incidelen and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs), despite their success in optical character recognition (OCR) tasks, are vulnerable to typographic attacks and have a fragile structure for images with multiple text layers. In this study, the DecoyBench dataset was created using the Decoy Font method. The dataset consists of 300 images, each containing text with sharp contour lines superimposed on another text with soft shading. Six recent closed-source models from three different model families were evaluated using this dataset under two different prompting conditions (naive and guided) and at two different resolutions ($512\times512$ and $64\times64$). A validation study showed that human participants could read both text layers with high accuracy. In contrast, the models, with most variants and both prompting methods, read the contour text with near-human accuracy at high resolution, but almost never fully extracted the shading text. At low resolution, the contour text could not be read by either the models or humans, while the shading text could be extracted with high accuracy. The findings indicate that the evaluated VLMs exhibit a consistent behavioral limitation when processing typographic structures containing multiple spatial frequency layers. Year 2026 Field NLP arXiv 2609.31403 PDF Download Categories cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.CV Abstract ​ Vision-language models (VLMs), despite their success in optical character recognition (OCR) tasks, are vulnerable to typographic attacks and have a fragile structure for images with multiple text layers. In this study, the DecoyBench dataset was created using the Decoy Font method. The dataset consists of 300 images, each containing text with sharp contour lines superimposed on another text with soft shading. Six recent closed-source models from three different model families were evaluated using this dataset under two different prompting conditions (naive and guided) and at two different resolutions ( 512 × 512 512\times512 512 × 512 and 64 × 64 64\times64 64 × 64 ). A validation study showed that human participants could read both text layers with high accuracy. In contrast, the models, with most variants and both prompting methods, read the contour text with near-human accuracy at high resolution, but almost never fully extracted the shading text. At low resolution, the contour text could not be read by either the models or humans, while the shading text could be extracted with high accuracy. The findings indicate that the evaluated VLMs exhibit a consistent behavioral limitation when processing typographic structures containing multiple spatial frequency layers. article.body:
Vision-language models miss one of two readable text layers in benchmark test

Researchers evaluated six closed-source vision-language models on reading layered text, a perception task relevant to robots, in the DecoyBench benchmark reported on 25 September 2026. The study describes no physical robot or sensing hardware, so it provides no joint, gripper, payload, reach or manipulation measurements. Models received naive or guided prompts; the paper does not report robot autonomy, teleoperation or training data for the evaluated systems. DecoyBench contained 300 images combining sharp-contour text with soft-shading text, tested at 512×512 and 64×64 pixels. At high resolution, most model variants read the contour layer but almost never fully extracted the shading layer; at low resolution, models and humans generally failed on contours while models extracted shading. This was an image benchmark, not a physical or deployed robot test.
